Tennis is a racket sport played on a rectangular court between two players in singles competition or four players in doubles. Players hit a felt-covered ball over a net to score points. The server must land serves in the service box, and rallies continue until a player fails to return the ball in bounds or makes an unforced error. The sport originated in twelfth-century France as a hand-striking game called jeu de paume and evolved into the modern lawn-tennis game in nineteenth-century England. It became an Olympic sport in 1896 and is the basis for the four Grand Slam tournaments: Wimbledon, the U.S. Open, the French Open, and the Australian Open. Tennis combines speed, strategy, endurance, and technical precision, and professional tennis has produced iconic athletes who dominated the sport and transcended it culturally.

Tennis scoring is unique. Within a game, points are counted as love, which is zero, then fifteen, thirty, forty, and game. A player must win by two if the score is tied at forty-forty, a situation called deuce. A set is won by the first player to win six games with a two-game lead, or via a tiebreak, which goes to the first player to seven points by a margin of two, if the score reaches six games to six. A match is typically best of three sets or best of five sets.

The four Grand Slam tournaments are the sport's most prestigious events. Wimbledon is played on grass courts in England. The French Open is played on clay courts in Paris. The U.S. Open is played on hard courts in New York. The Australian Open is played on hard courts in Melbourne. Winning all four in a single calendar year is called the Calendar Grand Slam. This has been achieved only twice: by Don Budge in 1938 and by Margaret Court in 1970.

Modern tennis evolved from jeu de paume, a French hand-striking game played indoors. When played outdoors on grass in the nineteenth century, players adopted rackets. Major Walter Clopton Wingfield codified the modern game in 1873, and it spread rapidly through the British Empire and America. The serve is critical to tennis success. A player gets two attempts to serve, and if both attempts miss the service box, it counts as two faults. A powerful and accurate serve provides a huge advantage. Legendary servers like Pete Sampras and Goran Ivanisevic often dominated opponents through their serve alone.

Tennis surfaces dramatically affect how the game is played. Grass at Wimbledon is fast and favors big servers and net-rushers. Clay at the French Open is slow and bouncy, favoring baseline rallies and footwork. Hard courts at the U.S. Open and Australian Open are intermediate in speed and provide consistent bounce.

Professional tennis was long segregated by sex and restricted to amateurs. Women could not play in most tournaments. The Open Era began in 1968 and allowed professionals to compete. Billie Jean King's advocacy was crucial to women's tennis. In 1973, she defeated Bobby Riggs in a match called the Battle of the Sexes, proving that women's tennis was compelling and commercially viable.

The sport has produced several transcendent champions. Roger Federer won twenty Grand Slams and set the standard for elegant, all-around play. Serena Williams won twenty-three Grand Slams and revolutionized women's tennis with power and athleticism. Novak Djokovic has won twenty-four Grand Slams using exceptional defensive consistency. Modern professional tennis is grueling. Top players compete in over seventy matches annually across continents. The mental and physical toll of the sport has driven innovations in training, nutrition, psychology, and equipment, including racket technology, string materials, and specialized footwear.
